claude.sample_unit: adults with type 1 diabetes (REPLACE trial CGM data)
models_evaluated: XGBoost hypoglycaemia risk model with SHAP explanations

links.outcome: Whether combining covariate shift, multiple performance metrics and feature importance detects drift and safety risk
links.effect: Combined monitoring identified different drift types; single metrics missed risks (e.g., +20 mg/dL shift showed no AUROC/AP drop but significant sensitivity drop); simplistic drift detection could misidentify risk.
links.quote: This underlines the importance of using multiple methods and metrics to track drift and hence model safety.

links.outcome: Model performance under perturbed inputs (sensor noise, uniform offsets, reduced CGM use)
links.effect: Adding 5% Gaussian noise significantly lowered AUROC, AP and sensitivity, with specificity sharply declining and hypoglycaemia overpredicted; ±20 mg/dL shifts produced significant changes.
links.quote: Any addition of noise significantly lowers model performance as marked by AUROC, AP and sensitivity.

links.outcome: Effect of anomalous or shifted input data on model outputs and covariate shift detection
links.effect: Even 5% noise gave normalised JS divergence of 172 sigma; sensor noise and offsets degraded performance and changed output rates.
links.quote: Even a modest addition of 5% noise leads to a very significant covariate shift.

links.outcome: Whether covariate shift (JS divergence) thresholds alone reliably signal performance degradation
links.effect: JS divergence did not track performance consistently: reduced CGM use gave large drift but only marginal performance change, and high variance pattern had high JS divergence with improved performance.
links.quote: Therefore, predictive performance is only marginally affected as CGM use drops, despite a significant drift in JS divergence.

links.outcome: Model performance when applied to unseen usage patterns, behaviours and sensor conditions
links.effect: Performance varied across glucose patterns; 'above range' users at elevated risk of false negatives, 'below range' had higher false-alarm rate, lowest CGM use (<0.1) significantly decreased performance.
links.quote: users who are ‘above range’ (3.2) despite only having a moderate covariate shift relative to baseline and no negative change in AUROC are at elevated risk of false negatives (ie, hypoglycaemia missed by the model).

links.outcome: Whether a single performance metric conceals poor performance under drift
links.effect: AUROC alone missed a significant sensitivity drop at +20 mg/dL shift; 'above range' AUROC rose while AP and sensitivity fell.
links.quote: This highlights the danger of using performance metrics alone to identify drift.

unlisted_practices: Bootstrap-normalised Jensen-Shannon divergence to compare covariate shift across samples of different size
Tracking SHAP feature importance shifts as a drift and explainability monitoring signal

openai.sample_unit: adults with type 1 diabetes using CGM

links.outcome: Covariate shift under Gaussian-noise stress test
links.effect: Mean JS: 0.00275 with no added noise, 0.144 at 5%, 0.209 at 10%, and 0.251 at 20% Gaussian noise.
links.quote: Even a modest addition of 5% noise leads to a very significant covariate shift.

links.outcome: Combined drift-monitoring framework
links.effect: Mean JS examples: behavior patterns 0.0091–0.1092, CGM-use bins 0.0119–0.0838, Gaussian-noise tests 0.00275–0.251.
links.quote: We demonstrate that using a combination of covariate shift detection, multiple performance metrics and feature importance offers a powerful methodology of identifying different types of drifts in sensor data.

links.outcome: Single-metric performance masking
links.effect: +20 mg/dL uniform shift: no notable AUROC or AP drop, but significant sensitivity drop.
links.quote: In particular, +20 mg/dL shows no notable drop in AUROC or AP; however, a significant drop in sensitivity.

links.outcome: Performance with low CGM use
links.effect: CGM use 0.0–0.1: mean JS 0.0838 and 113.17σ; 0.7–0.8: mean JS 0.0119 and 12.44σ; <0.1 significantly decreased performance.
links.quote: Only the lowest usage fraction (<0.1) results in a significant decrease in model performance.

links.outcome: Explanation instability under sensor noise
links.effect: As Gaussian noise increased to 5%, 10%, and 20%, mean JS rose to 0.144, 0.209, and 0.251, with rate-of-change SD gaining importance.
links.quote: There is a strong correlation with the amplitude of added noise and the importance of ‘SD of rate of change’ features.

links.outcome: Performance after sensor/device noise
links.effect: Gaussian sensor noise: mean JS 0.144 at 5%, 0.209 at 10%, 0.251 at 20%; performance degradation was significant with any added noise.
links.quote: For device and sensor changes, adding noise results in large covariate shifts, significant performance degradation and a change in the importance of rate of change (of CGM readings).

links.outcome: hypoglycemia prediction performance under sensor calibration shift
links.effect: A +20 mg/dL shift showed no notable drop in AUROC or AP, but caused a significant drop in sensitivity.
links.quote: In particular, +20 mg/dL shows no notable drop in AUROC or AP; however, a significant drop in sensitivity.

unlisted_practices: Combining covariate shift detection, multiple performance metrics, and feature attribution explainability to monitor and interpret data drift in sensor-based predictive models

screen.practice: drift monitoring (covariate shift detection, performance metrics, feature importance)
screen.reason: Evaluates methods for drift monitoring (covariate shift detection, performance metrics, and feature importance shifts) under simulated real-world sensor and behavioral changes to ensure ongoing safety of glucose risk prediction models.
